title: NP outside BQP
formal:
Is \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\)? That is, does there exist a total decision language
\[L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\quad\text{with}\quad L\in\mathrm{NP}\ \text{and}\ L\notin\mathrm{BQP}?\]
Equivalently, is the total language \(3\text{-}\mathrm{SAT}\) defined below outside \(\mathrm{BQP}\)? The negation is that every language with polynomially bounded classical certificates and a polynomial-time classical verifier has a uniform bounded-error quantum polynomial-time decider. This is noncontainment, not merely inequality of two classes.
definitions:
A language is a set of finite binary strings. Put \(n=|x|\) and write \(\mathbf1_L(x)\) for its membership bit, allowing \(n=0\). The condition \(L\in\mathrm{NP}\) means that there exist a finite deterministic classical multitape Turing-machine verifier \(V\) and fixed positive integers \(C,d,K,e\) such that
\[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{*},\quad |y|\le C(n+1)^d\ \land\ V(x,y)=1.\]
For every pair of binary strings \((x,y)\), the verifier halts with a bit output within \(K(|x|+|y|+1)^e\) ordinary tape steps. The existentially quantified certificate is classical. It defines membership but is not supplied to the quantum decider, which receives only \(x\). All programs and exponents are fixed independently of the input length.

The condition \(L\in\mathrm{BQP}\) is defined using circuits over the fixed gates \(H,T,\mathrm{CNOT}\). In the ordered one-qubit basis \((|0\rangle,|1\rangle)\),
\[H=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&(1+i)/\sqrt2\end{pmatrix},\qquad i^2=-1.\]
On two distinct addressed qubits, \(\mathrm{CNOT}|a,b\rangle=|a,a\mathbin{\oplus}b\rangle\) for bits \(a,b\), where \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. Gates act as the identity on all other qubits. They may address any qubits; there is no geometric locality restriction.

There must exist one deterministic classical multitape Turing machine \(G\) and fixed positive integers \(K,e\) such that, on unary input \(1^n\), including the empty unary string at \(n=0\), \(G\) prints within \(K(n+1)^e\) bit steps a complete circuit description. The description specifies a register size \(q(n)\ge n+1\), an ordered list of \(m(n)\) gates with binary qubit addresses, and one designated output qubit \(j(n)\). Both \(q(n)\) and \(m(n)\) are at most \(K(n+1)^e\). Every listed address must be valid, and the list depends only on \(n\), not on the particular \(x\). The circuit may have unrestricted depth subject to this polynomial gate bound.

For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), initialize the register to the computational basis state \(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{q(n)-n}\rangle\). A computational basis state \(|y\rangle\) is the unit coordinate vector indexed by \(y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}\) in \(\mathbb C^{2^{q(n)}}\). Apply the listed unitary matrices in order, obtaining
\[|\psi_x\rangle=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{q(n)}}\alpha_y|y\rangle,
\qquad \sum_y|\alpha_y|^2=1.\]
Measure only qubit \(j(n)\) at the end. The probability of output \(b\in\{0,1\}\) is exactly \(\sum_{y:y_{j(n)}=b}|\alpha_y|^2\). For every \(x\), this probability must be at least \(2/3\) when \(b=\mathbf1_L(x)\). These equations specify the mathematical semantics; the machine is not asked to write down the exponentially long state vector or its amplitudes.

There is no advice, oracle gate, postselection, supplied quantum state or freely chosen real parameter. All auxiliary qubits start at zero. Only the stated finite gate set is primitive; gate descriptions and uniform generation are finite classical data. Quantum computation is ideal; hardware noise is outside the model. Constants and exponents may depend on the fixed language's algorithms, but not on \(n\) or \(x\).

For a concrete satisfiability language, a formula has variables \(z_1,\ldots,z_N\) and \(M\) explicitly listed clauses. Each clause has zero to three literals, each a variable or its negation. A truth assignment is a vector in \(\{0,1\}^{N}\); it satisfies a clause when at least one literal is true and satisfies the formula when every clause is satisfied. The empty conjunction is true and an empty clause is false; repeated variables, repeated clauses and tautologies are allowed.

Here is one explicit binary representation. For an integer \(u\ge0\), let \(b(u)\) be its binary expansion without leading zeros, with \(b(0)=0\), and put \(B(u)=1^{|b(u)|}0b(u)\). Begin with \(1^N0B(M)\). For each of the \(M\) clauses, write \(B(k)\) for its length \(0\le k\le3\), followed by its \(k\) literals. A literal is a sign bit and \(B(j)\) for \(1\le j\le N\); sign zero denotes \(z_j\), sign one denotes \(\neg z_j\). There are no trailing bits. The language \(3\text{-}\mathrm{SAT}\) consists of the valid encodings with a satisfying assignment. Every malformed string is a no-instance. Input length counts every encoding bit, rather than only \(N\), and the unary variable-count field ensures that the full assignment has polynomial length in the encoding.

This encoding is polynomially equivalent to the usual explicit 3-CNF satisfiability problem, with variables relabeled consecutively when necessary. By NP-completeness and closure of BQP under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions, \(3\text{-}\mathrm{SAT}\in\mathrm{BQP}\) is equivalent to \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\). A many-one reduction here is one deterministic polynomial-time map \(f\) with \(x\in L\) exactly when \(f(x)\) is a satisfiable valid encoding. This equivalence concerns total languages, with the required bounded error on every yes- and no-instance.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of either
\[\exists L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*},\quad L\in\mathrm{NP}\land L\notin\mathrm{BQP},\]
or its full negation \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\).

A separation must establish the classical verifier and polynomial certificate bound for one fixed language and exclude every polynomial-time-uniform quantum circuit family with any fixed polynomial size/register bounds in the stated finite-gate model. Equivalently, it may prove that the full encoded 3-SAT language is outside BQP. A containment proof may instead give a uniform quantum decider for this 3-SAT language, including rejection of malformed encodings, and establish its complete resource and pointwise success guarantees together with the NP-completeness implication.

An oracle or unstructured-search lower bound does not exclude algorithms that inspect the explicit input. Neither a restriction to selected formula families nor a lower bound for one quantum architecture answers the full question. Merely proving \(\mathrm{NP}\ne\mathrm{BQP}\) is insufficient if the argument only places a language in BQP outside NP. A proposed SAT algorithm must count all elementary operations and qubits, including state preparation and any subroutine implementation. Nonlinear dynamics, postselection, supplied witnesses or uncharged exponential resources are outside this BQP definition. There is no unproved hardness assumption or numerical approximation tolerance in the target.
why: This asks whether efficient classical verification always permits efficient quantum decision. Noncontainment would identify a limit even for ideal scalable quantum computers and would also imply P differs from NP. Containment would place all classically verifiable decision problems within quantum polynomial time.

importance.reason: A foundational relation between quantum algorithms and NP-completeness; a noncontainment proof would also separate P from NP.

progress.text: Quantum factoring and discrete-logarithm algorithms establish important polynomial-time upper bounds for structured function problems.
Grover establishes \(O(\sqrt M)\) query search, a quadratic improvement in the number of candidates rather than a general polynomial-time SAT result.
Bennett–Bernstein–Brassard–Vazirani give quantum lower bounds relative to random oracles and explicitly distinguish them from ordinary NP noncontainment.
The inspected book edition records \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\) as Conjecture 11.4.
The large-Pauli-coefficient reduction transfers NP noncontainment to a promised quantum-state task as a hardness assumption.
A revised Valiant–Vazirani paper discusses a nonlinear coprocessor model; that extra operation is outside ordinary BQP.

status_note: Source-open evidence checked through 16 September 2026. The inspected 2019 source states NP noncontainment in BQP as Conjecture 11.4, and the June 2026 Pauli-coefficient paper uses it as an unproved hardness assumption. The checked oracle lower bounds, formula-oracle synthesis and nonlinear-coprocessor results do not settle the stated total-language comparison in the standard finite-gate model. Bounded current searches located neither a matching unconditional noncontainment proof nor a general BQP SAT algorithm. This review does not independently certify every cited proof or exhaust all later literature.

context_blocks.text: For a satisfiable formula, one assignment certifies a yes answer; for an unsatisfiable formula, every assignment fails. The quantum decider receives the formula without a certificate and must answer both cases reliably. Its input is the entire explicit syntax, so shared variables and clause structure are available to every algorithm being quantified over.

Since deterministic polynomial-time computation is contained in BQP, \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\) implies \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\). A proof merely that classical deterministic computation is weaker than NP would not by itself establish this stronger noncontainment. The statement also differs from BPP versus BQP: quantum algorithms could be more powerful than classical randomization while still failing on some NP languages.

Shor’s factoring and discrete-logarithm algorithms are polynomial in the input bit length. These structured function tasks do not provide a general quantum decider for every NP language, and their quantum upper bounds do not prove any unrestricted classical lower bound. They are major algorithmic successes whose scope remains distinct from the NP-complete decision target.

For unstructured search over \(M\) candidates with one marked candidate, Grover’s bound is \(O(\sqrt M)\) oracle queries. With \(N\) binary assignment coordinates, the square-root search scale \(\sqrt{2^N}=2^{N/2}\) is still exponential in \(N\); evaluating a candidate also has a cost. This resource comparison does not establish a lower bound for all algorithms on an explicitly supplied formula.

Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard and Vazirani prove that relative to a randomly chosen length-preserving oracle, with probability one NP is not contained in bounded-error quantum time \(o(2^{n/2})\). Both the quantum algorithm and the NP verifier receive the oracle. The source expressly warns that its oracle theorem does not rule out unrelativized \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\). Black-box evaluations reveal less structure than a full formula description.

Cifuentes’ June 2026 preprint studies whether a circuit-prepared state has a nonidentity Pauli observable with expectation magnitude at least \(\varepsilon\), promised against all such magnitudes being at most \(\varepsilon/2\). Pauli observables are tensor products of the standard one-qubit identity and Pauli matrices. Its reduction shows that an efficient quantum solver for this promise task would imply \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{BQP}\), even for pure states and thresholds bounded below by a positive constant. The resulting hardness is conditional on this card’s conjecture; it does not prove the conjecture.

Kelly and coauthors’ June 2026 revision discusses efficient SAT solving with an added nonlinear quantum coprocessor. Its first section explicitly distinguishes those dynamics from the usual linear unitary circuit model and notes the exponential space cost of the discussed large-system simulation. Consequently, its proposed computational power is not a BQP algorithm under the gate and qubit bounds specified here.

sentences: NP consists of total decision languages with polynomial-length classical certificates checkable in deterministic polynomial time.
The question is whether at least one such language has no uniform bounded-error quantum polynomial-time decider, equivalently whether full 3-SAT is outside BQP.
The quantum model has a fixed finite universal gate set, polynomially many zero-initialized auxiliary qubits and a final membership-bit measurement, with no supplied witness or oracle.
Structured quantum algorithms and unstructured-search or oracle lower bounds do not settle the unrestricted explicit-input comparison.
Recent Pauli-coefficient hardness remains conditional on this noncontainment, while nonlinear quantum computation adds operations outside the model.

source_formulation.text: The standard noncontainment target is retained. In the inspected 6 August 2019 Wigderson draft it is Conjecture 11.4; the inherited March 2018 edition used Conjecture 11.5. The nearby BPP-versus-BQP conjecture is a different class comparison. The explicit NP verifier, finite-gate BQP semantics and 3-SAT encoding clarify the existing question without replacing it by a promise, search or restricted-circuit problem.
